title: Vizio smart TVs tracked what people watched
hook: The TV was watching you back, second by second.
collected: Second-by-second information about what was shown on the screen, from broadcast, cable and streaming sources.
howObtained: Automatic content recognition (ACR) software that matched screen pixels against a database, switched on by default.
inferred: Viewing habits, linked to household details such as age, income and marital status, according to the FTC.
done: The FTC and New Jersey alleged Vizio sold viewing histories to third parties for advertising and audience measurement without telling viewers or getting consent.
affected: Owners of Vizio smart TVs. The FTC's headline refers to 11 million TVs; that is a count of TVs, not a confirmed count of people tracked.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC and New Jersey court order. No admission of wrongdoing.

outcome.text: $2.2 million ($1.5 million to the FTC; $1 million to New Jersey, $300,000 of it suspended), plus consent and deletion requirements.

sources.title: VIZIO to Pay $2.2 Million to FTC, State of New Jersey

limits: An older case; TV makers have changed defaults since, but ACR remains common.
whyItMatters: Smart TVs are subsidised partly by the data they gather about you.

title: Researchers measured smart-TV content recognition on Samsung and LG
hook: ACR kept working even when the TV was just a screen for a laptop.
collected: Snapshots of what is on screen, sent to the TV maker's content-recognition servers.
howObtained: ACR built into the TV, on by default.
inferred: What you watch, including content from devices plugged into the TV.
done: Anselmi et al. ('Watching TV with the Second-Party', IMC 2024) audited Samsung and LG TVs in the UK and US. ACR ran on live TV and on input from external devices (HDMI), not on apps like Netflix; opting out stopped the traffic.
affected: Owners of these TVs with default settings.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Peer-reviewed measurement study (ACM Internet Measurement Conference).

sources.title: Watching TV with the Second-Party: A First Look at Automatic Content Recognition Tracking in Smart TVs

limits: Two brands, two countries, specific models.
whyItMatters: The opt-out works, but only if you know it exists. It is on by default.

title: Texas sues five TV makers over content recognition
hook: The state claims TVs captured what was on screen as often as every half second.
collected: Screen contents, according to the lawsuits.
done: Texas's attorney general sued Sony, Samsung, LG, Hisense and TCL, alleging the TVs captured screen contents (reportedly every 500 milliseconds on some models) and used dark patterns to get consent.
label: ALLEGED
labelNote: Lawsuits filed; no court has ruled.

companyResponse.text: Hisense and LG declined to comment on pending litigation; TCL and Sony declined to comment.

sources.title: Texas sues 5 smart TV makers over ACR tech

limits: The capture intervals are the state's claims and differ between reports.
whyItMatters: Regulators are returning to the TV in the living room.

title: Amazon: Alexa kept children's voice recordings; Ring staff could view customers' videos
hook: Data kept 'to improve the service' was used to train algorithms.
collected: Children's voice recordings and location data from Alexa; private home video from Ring cameras.
howObtained: Smart speakers and home security cameras.
inferred: Not the main issue. The cases were about keeping and accessing the data.
done: The FTC and DOJ alleged Amazon kept children's Alexa recordings indefinitely, undermined deletion requests, and used them to train its algorithms. Separately, the FTC alleged Ring let employees and contractors access customers' private videos.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC/DOJ orders. Amazon disagreed with the claims and denied breaking the law.

companyResponse.text: Amazon said it disagreed with the FTC's claims and denied violating the law, but that the settlements put these matters behind it.

outcome.text: $25 million (Alexa, children's privacy law) and $5.8 million (Ring).

sources.title: FTC and DOJ Charge Amazon with Violating Children's Privacy Law by Keeping Kids' Alexa Voice Recordings Forever
Amazon will pay $25 million in FTC child data privacy fine

limits: Settled. No finding that recordings were used for ads.
whyItMatters: 'Delete' should mean delete. Keeping data longer creates new uses for it.

title: Siri accidental recordings class action ($95 million)
hook: Users claimed private conversations led to ads. Apple settled but denies it.
collected: Audio recorded when Siri activated by mistake, without the wake word.
inferred: Plaintiffs claimed overheard words (for example brand names or a surgery) were used to target ads.
done: Plaintiffs in Lopez v. Apple alleged accidental recordings were captured and shared with contractors, and some claimed they then saw related ads.
affected: US Siri users in the class period.
label: ALLEGED
labelNote: Private class-action settlement, not a regulator finding. The ad-targeting claims were never proven. That contractors reviewed some Siri recordings was widely reported in 2019.

companyResponse.text: Apple settled to avoid further litigation and said Siri data has never been used to build marketing profiles or sold.

outcome.text: $95 million proposed settlement; we did not confirm final approval.

sources.title: Apple Siri settlement: who is eligible
Apple offers $95M to settle Siri privacy lawsuit

limits: A settlement is not proof. See the Myths room on 'your phone is listening'.
whyItMatters: A good test of the difference between 'they recorded by accident' and 'they listen to sell ads'.

title: A marketing firm's 'Active Listening' pitch
hook: A sales deck claimed ads could be targeted from what device microphones overhear.
collected: Claimed: voice data picked up by device microphones.
howObtained: Not explained in any technical detail.
done: 404 Media published a Cox Media Group pitch deck claiming it could target ads using 'Active Listening' and listing Google, Meta and Amazon as partners.
affected: Unknown; no technical evidence it worked.
label: STATEMENT
labelNote: A company's own sales claim. No technical evidence was shown that it works or was deployed.

companyResponse.text: Google removed CMG from its Partners Program. Meta said it does not use your phone's microphone for ads and was reviewing CMG. Amazon said it has never worked with CMG on this program.
companyResponse.source: Company statements reported by 404 Media and others

sources.title: Here's the Pitch Deck for 'Active Listening' Ad Targeting

limits: Marketing claims are not evidence of capability.
whyItMatters: Teaches the difference between a pitch and a proof.
